Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.

Key Features

💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.

AKS and Azure Product Retirements

Retirement notices for products tracked by this page. Dates and actions come from Microsoft Azure Updates.

Azure Kubernetes Service—Retiring support for Kubernetes versions 1.11 and 1.12

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT December 9, 2019 Notice updated: 2019-09-30
Full notice and recommended action
On Monday, December 9, 2019 (2019-12-09), we’re removing support for Kubernetes versions older than the latest version (N), and two minor versions prior (N-2), because support for Kubernetes 1.15 will become available on that date. Customers running Kubernetes versions older than Kubernetes 1.13.x must upgrade by Monday, December 9, 2019, to remain in support. After that date, customers will be asked to upgrade to a supported version when they open new Azure support requests. Please note: this date is specific to AKS and isn’t related to any upstream or community dates for Kubernetes 1.15.

We’re making this change now to align more closely with the upstream Kubernetes project, and to provide a more consistent experience for customers with regards to bug fixes, security patches, and component compatibility.

With this change, AKS will support the current generally available Kubernetes release and the two previous minor versions (N-2). Historically, AKS has supported the current generally available release of Kubernetes, as well as the three prior minor versions (N-3). When a new minor version is released, the oldest minor version is removed.

After Monday, December 9, 2019, the supported Kubernetes minor releases will be:

- 1.13.x

- 1.14.x

- 1.15.x

To verify what versions are available in your region:

```

az aks get-upgrades --resource-group myResourceGroup --name myAKSCluster --output table

```

To upgrade your clusters using the Azure CLI:

```

az aks upgrade --resource-group myResourceGroup --name myAKSCluster --kubernetes-version <NEW VERSION>

```

For additional information, please see the AKS Kubernetes support policy.

If you have questions, please contact us.

Azure Container Service Will Retire on January 31, 2020

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT January 31, 2020 Notice updated: 2018-12-05
Full notice and recommended action
In 2017, we introduced Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) for simplifying Kubernetes management, deployment, and operations. Because it fully replaces Azure Container Service (ACS) capabilities for Kubernetes, ACS will be retired as a standalone service on January 31, 2020.

If you use the Kubernetes orchestrator, please migrate to AKS by January 31, 2020. We encourage you to make the switch sooner to take advantage of these feature enhancements:

·     Simplified deployment of managed Kubernetes clusters in Azure.

·     Reduced complexity and operational overhead of managing Kubernetes.

·     Critical tasks like health monitoring and maintenance are handled by AKS.

If you use ACS with Docker or DC/OS, please migrate to a solution template as recommended below.

How this will affect you

Beginning January 31, 2020, all ACS APIs will be blocked. Additionally, you’ll no longer be able to create new clusters, update, or scale existing clusters using the portal, CLI, or Resource Manager templates. However, you’ll still be able to list and delete existing clusters using these client tools. While the existing clusters and the applications running on them should continue to work after January 31, 2020, there will be no technical support available or feature improvements.

The acs-engine project used for creating unmanaged container orchestrator clusters has also been deprecated and will no longer see active development. Instead, we have migrated the Kubernetes portion of that project to a new repo, aks-engine and will continue the open-source work backing Kubernetes on Azure there. As with ACS, existing clusters deployed via acs-engine should continue to run and aks-engine will offer backward compatibility for scale and upgrade operations. For new clusters, we encourage you to move to using aks-engine.

Recommended action

Migrate from ACS to one of the following options no later than January 31, 2020:

If you use ACS with Kubernetes, migrate to Azure Kubernetes Service or to the aks-engine open-source project.

If you use ACS with Docker, move to the Basic or Standard/Advanced Docker Enterprise Edition for Azure solution template.

If you use ACS with DC/OS, move to the Mesosphere DC/OS Enterprise or Mesosphere DC/OS Open Source solution template.

Still have questions? Contact us.

Retirement: Transition from Helm Repositories to OCI Artifacts for Storing Helm Charts

Azure Container Registry
View notice
RETIREMENT March 30, 2025 Notice updated: 2024-09-26
Full notice and recommended action
In November 2020, Helm v2 reached end of life. Starting March 30th, 2025, Azure Container Registry will no longer support Helm v2. Therefore, the legacy “Helm repositories” functionality will also be retired. After this date, Azure Container Registry will only support storing Helm charts as Open Container Initiative (OCI) Artifacts.
Open Container Initiative (OCI) Artifacts are container artifacts that utilize the OCI image specification. This allows you to store a Helm chart as an artifact inside your registry by running a `helm push` command and install a Helm chart by running a `helm install` command. You can check out a complete guide on working with Helm charts stored as an OCI Artifact here: Store Helm charts - Azure Container Registry | Microsoft Learn

How does this affect me?

- Starting October 30, 2024, the CLI command `az acr helm push` will be retired. This will prevent pushing new helm charts to legacy helm repositories.
- Starting March 30, 2025, the CLI command group `az acr helm` will be retired. This will end all legacy helm repository capabilities in Azure Container Registry.
- All Helm charts not stored as an OCI Artifact will be deleted from Azure Container Registry March 30th, 2025.
- Learn how to find all Helm Charts stored in a Helm repository here: az acr helm | Microsoft Learn. If the Helm Chart you are using is listed then it is stored in a legacy Helm repository and is at risk of deletion.

Required Action

- If you haven’t already, you must begin to migrate to Helm v3. You can find more detailed information in the Helm documentation: Helm | Migrating Helm v2 to v3
- Once you are using Helm v3, you can push your Helm charts as OCI Artifacts. You can read about how to do this in the Azure Container Registry documentation: Store Helm charts - Azure Container Registry | Microsoft Learn

Retirement: Upgrade your Azure HDInsight clusters with TLS versions 1 dot 1 and below by March 31, 2025

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT March 31, 2025 Notice updated: 2025-01-29
Full notice and recommended action
Customers that have Azure HDInsight cluster is using TLS version 1.1 or lower are requested to upgrade to clusters have TLS version 1.2.  

To enhance security and provide best-in-class encryption for your data, we'll require all connections to Azure HDInsight clusters to be secured using Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2 or later beginning March 31, 2025, when connectivity will only be available through TLS 1.2 or later versions. This retirement notice applies only to Azure HDInsight clusters; all other TLS retirements aren’t impacted by this announcement.    

Your clusters maybe configured to use TLS 1.1 or lower due to outdated clusters, or other applications connected to Azure HDInsight clusters that only support lower TLS versions.  

Required action  

Upgrade to versions 5.1 of the Azure HDInsight cluster with TLS version 1.2 by March 31 to keep your clusters working as expected. To avoid potential service disruptions, confirm that your resources that interact with Azure services are using TLS 1.2 or later.  

-
If they're already exclusively using TLS 1.2 or later, you don't need to take further action.  

-
If they still have a dependency on TLS 1.0 or 1.1, transition them to TLS 1.2 or later.   

If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, create a support request .

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026:
- Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools.
- AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools.
- Existing node pools won’t receive security patches.

On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options:
- Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade.
- Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools.

For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Retirement notice: Windows Server 2022 will retire with k8s 1.34 in March 2027

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT March 15, 2027 Notice updated: 2024-03-29
Full notice and recommended action
On 15 March 2027, Windows Server 2022 will be retired when Kubernetes 1.34 reaches the end of platform support. You will not be able to create new Windows Server 2022 node pools on Kubernetes 1.35 and above. We encourage you to make the switch before 15 March 2027 to gain the richer benefits of Windows Server 2025 or Windows Server Annual Channel. These new Windows OS versions will be supported on AKS before Windows Server 2022 is retired. For more updates, see our AKS public roadmap.  

Required action

From now through 14 March 2027, you can continue to use Windows Server 2022 on Kubernetes version 1.34 and below. After 15 March 2027, Windows Server 2022 won't be supported. You won’t be able to create Windows Server 2022 node pools on Kubernetes 1.35 and above. Follow the detailed steps in our documentation to upgrade to a supported Windows Server version (Windows Server 2025 or Windows Server Annual Channel) by 15 March 2027.   

Help and Support

If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and you need technical help, please create a support request.

Retirement: Deprecation of sidecar for remote-write for Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT March 31, 2027 Notice updated: 2026-03-30
Full notice and recommended action
On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity.

We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup.

We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service.

If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

Retirement: Open Service Mesh add-on for AKS will be retired on September 30, 2027

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT September 30, 2027 Notice updated: 2024-09-26
Full notice and recommended action
Following the archival of the Open Service Mesh project, the Istio service mesh add-on was released for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) and is Generally Available since February 28,2024. 

Due to the upstream archival of open-source Open Service Mesh, the Open Service Mesh add-on for AKS will no longer receive any new minor version releases or new features and will be retired on September 30, 2027. Security patch updates will be provided up until September 30, 2027.

You can continue to use the existing Open Service Mesh add-on for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) until September 30, 2027 or transition to Istio add-on for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) before that time. Migration guidance from Open Service Mesh (OSM) configurations to Istio can be found here. There are no changes in pricing between the two add-ons.

Retirement: Open Service Mesh extension for Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on September 30, 2027

RETIREMENT September 30, 2027 Notice updated: 2024-09-26
Full notice and recommended action
Following the archival of the upstream open-source Open Service Mesh project in upstream open source, the Open Service Mesh extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will no longer receive any new minor version releases or new features and will be retired on 30 September 30, 2027. Security patch updates will be provided up until September 30, 2027.

You can continue to use the existing Open Service Mesh extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes until September 30, 2027 or transition to an open-source alternative such as Istio before that time. Migration guidance from Open Service Mesh (OSM) configurations to Istio can be found here.

Retirement: Pod name dimension in AKS pod platform metrics

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT September 30, 2027 Notice updated: 2026-10-06
Full notice and recommended action
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure
Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters:

- Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase)
- Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready)

After this change:
- Metric names remain unchanged.
- Aggregate pod counts remain available.
- Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported.
- The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting.

During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement.
You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow:

- Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension.
- Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension.

Recommended action:

- If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required.
- If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure
Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native
pod metrics.

Help and support
If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Retirement: Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc enabled Kubernetes clusters

Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes
View notice
RETIREMENT October 9, 2027 Notice updated: 2026-10-09
Full notice and recommended action
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027.

Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster.

After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support.

Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Retirement: Docker Content Trust on March 31, 2028 – Replaced by the Notary Project and Azure Key Vault

Azure Container Registry
View notice
RETIREMENT March 31, 2028 Notice updated: 2025-03-26
Full notice and recommended action
Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation.

How does this affect me?

- Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry.
- Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028.
- Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028.

Required Action

Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started.

Signing:

- Use AKV with self-signed certificates
- Use AKV with CA-issued certificates
- Sign in ADO pipelines
- Sign in GitHub workflows

Verification:

- Verify in ADO pipelines
- Verify in GitHub workflows
- Verify on AKS

Retirement: Kubenet Networking for Azure Kubernetes Service to Be Retired on March 31, 2028

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT March 31, 2028 Notice updated: 2025-03-18
Full notice and recommended action
On March 31, 2028, kubenet networking for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) will be retired.

To avoid service disruptions, you'll need to follow these instructions to upgrade to Azure Container Networking Interface (CNI) overlay before that date, when workloads running on kubenet for AKS will no longer be supported.

Azure CNI overlay provides the same IP address overlay architecture as kubenet, plus new capabilities for increased scalability. We encourage you to migrate to Azure CNI overlay prior to the retirement date to take advantage of the added benefits.

Retirement: Azure Network Policy Manager (NPM) for Linux nodes on AKS to Be Retired by September 30, 2028

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT September 30, 2028 Notice updated: 2025-10-01
Full notice and recommended action
On September 30, 2028, we’ll end support for Azure Network Policy Manager (NPM) on Linux nodes in AKS. To avoid disruptions, migrate AKS clusters running Linux nodes from NPM to Cilium Network Policy by that date.   

   

Transitioning to Cilium Network Policy for AKS clusters using Azure CNI powered by Cilium provides significant improvements, including:  

-
Robust support for Kubernetes-native policies.  

-
Powerful extended features such as Layer 7 policy, and Fully Qualified Domain Name filtering.  

-
eBPF-based architecture for packet processing, offering better performance, scalability and security.   

  

To view your impacted resources, go to the Azure Resource Graph and click Run query.  

Help and support 

If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A. If you have a support plan and need technical help, please submit a support request.

Pod Security Policy is being deprecated with AKS 1.25 and 2023-06-01 API version

AKS
View notice
RETIREMENT October 2025 Notice updated: 2023-12-02
Full notice and recommended action
Pod Security Policy (preview) is removed in AKS version 1.25 and retired on 1st August 2023 with AKS version 1.24 retirement. 

An AKS cluster with Pod Security Policy (preview) enabled can not be upgraded to AKS version 1.25+. 

Required action 

We recommend you migrate to pod security admission controller or Azure policy to stay within Azure support. Pod Security Admission is a built-in policy solution for single cluster implementations. If you are looking for enterprise-grade policy, then Azure policy is a better choice. 

 

You can also disable Pod Security Policy (preview) on existing clusters to upgrade to AKS version 1.25+ 

 

More information 

-

Pod Security Policy 

-

Pod Security Admission 

-

Azure policy 

-

Kubernetes announcement 

If you have additional questions, please contact us.

                                                                          @@ -2,13 +2,6 @@  This article provides best practices for monitoring and interpreting GPU signals on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). Instead of looking at NVIDIA GPU metrics in isolation, you correlate signals across utilization, memory, and workload context to improve long-term performance and node efficiency. -Important--AKS preview features are available on a self-service, opt-in basis. Previews are provided "as is" and "as available," and they're excluded from the service-level agreements and limited warranty. AKS previews are partially covered by customer support on a best-effort basis. As such, these features aren't meant for production use. For more information, see the following support articles:--- [AKS support policies](/en-us/azure/aks/support-policies)-- [Azure support FAQ](/en-us/azure/aks/faq)- ## Understand GPU utilization versus saturation  Don't treat the NVIDIA DCGM metric `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` as a direct efficiency score. `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` only indicates how often kernels are active, so it doesn't tell you whether the workload is compute-efficient. You get more accurate guidance by correlating utilization signals instead of reading them independently. Compare `DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL` with `DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE`, and then compare `DCGM_FI_PROF_SM_ACTIVE` with `DCGM_FI_PROF_DRAM_ACTIVE` to identify whether your bottleneck is compute, memory, or launch and synchronization overhead.

                                                                                          AKS - Azure Container Linux Overview

                                                                                          Operations ✨ Update Detected: 2026-11-07 08:30 UTC
                                                                                          Summary

                                                                                          The article provides an overview of Azure Container Linux (ACL) for AKS, detailing its general availability, benefits, and key features. It includes important migration information regarding the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard and outlines unsupported features for ACL.

                                                                                            View Documentation
                                                                                            Show changesHide changes (24 added, 28 removed lines)

                                                                                            Net changes between saved snapshots in this tracking window, shown as source Markdown. Publication metadata is excluded. + marks additions; - marks removals. Surrounding lines provide context.

                                                                                            @@ -2,51 +2,47 @@  In this article, we provide an overview of Azure Container Linux (ACL), an immutable, container-optimized operating system (OS) for Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). ACL is derived from the Flatcar Container Linux project, building on Flatcar's proven, container-first immutable design while layering in Azure Linux packages, servicing, and platform integration. This allows ACL to stay closely aligned with upstream Flatcar innovation while meeting Azure's production, security, and compliance requirements. To learn more about Flatcar Container Linux, see the [Flatcar documentation](https://www.flatcar.org/). -ACL is generally available (GA) as an OS option on AKS starting AKS v1.34. You can deploy ACL node pools in a new AKS cluster, add ACL node pools to your existing clusters, and migrate existing Linux node pools to ACL.+ACL is generally available (GA) as an OS option on AKS starting AKS v1.34. You can deploy ACL node pools in a new AKS cluster or add ACL node pools to your existing clusters. -Note+Important -ACL is the GA release of Flatcar Container Linux for AKS, which entered preview in November 2025. OS Guard (preview) features, such as code integrity with Integrity Policy Enforcement (IPE), currently aren't supported. If you need OS Guard features today, we recommend continuing to use OS Guard and migrating to ACL once those features become available.+Starting on **December 10, 2026**, Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) no longer supports Azure Linux with OS Guard for AKS (preview). At that point, AKS no longer produces new Azure Linux with OS Guard node images or provides security patches, and you can no longer create new node pools with Azure Linux with OS Guard. On **March 10, 2027**, AKS removes all existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node images, which causes scaling and remediation (reimage and redeploy) operations to fail. To avoid disruption, migrate to [Azure Container Linux (ACL)](azure-container-linux-overview). For more information about this retirement, see the [Retirement GitHub issue](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/issues/5950) and the [Azure Updates retirement announcement](https://azure.microsoft.com/updates/?id=571257). To stay informed about announcements and updates, follow the [AKS release notes](https://github.com/Azure/AKS/releases).  ## Benefits of using ACL on AKS -Using ACL as the OS for your AKS node pools provides several benefits that enhance security, reliability, and operational efficiency:+ACL is a secure, minimal OS that includes only the critical components required to run containers. It uses an immutable design to preserve OS integrity and reduce node configuration drift. -- **Built-in immutability for stronger security**: Kernel-enforced immutability of the `/usr` directory verifies the integrity of the OS image at boot and runtime. This design helps block unauthorized changes before they can affect your cluster and reduces the risk of OS-level tampering.-- **Minimal attack surface**: ACL ships only the components required to run containers. By reducing the size and complexity of the OS, ACL minimizes the number of packages, services, and potential entry points available to attackers and simplifies security management.-- **Automated node image updates**: ACL delivers weekly image-based updates that include the latest security patches and bug fixes. This approach keeps node OS versions consistent and current across the cluster and helps reduce exposure to known vulnerabilities.-- **Supply-chain trust**: Builds on Azure Linux’s signed packages and supply-chain processes, delivering clear provenance for system components.-- **Integration with Azure security features**: Native support for [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/aks/use-trusted-launch) and Secure Boot provides measured boot protections and attestation.-- **Open-source transparency**: Flatcar as well as many of the underlying technologies (dm-verity and SELinux) are upstream or open source, and Microsoft has tooling and contributions to support these features.+| Benefit | Description |+| --- | --- |+| **Layered OS security** | ACL combines an immutable OS, mandatory access controls, verified boot, and trusted build processes to protect nodes from boot through runtime. For details, see [ACL security features](/en-us/articles/azure-linux/azure-container-linux-security-features.md). |+| **Minimal container host** | ACL includes only the components required to run containers, reducing OS complexity and simplifying node management. |+| **Consistent node servicing** | Weekly image-based updates provide security patches and bug fixes while keeping the OS version consistent across each node image. |+| **Open-source transparency** | Flatcar as well as many of the underlying technologies (dm-verity and SELinux) are upstream or open source, and Microsoft has tooling and contributions to support these features. | -## Key features of ACL+## Capabilities and compatibility -The following key features distinguish ACL as a hardened, container-optimized OS for AKS:+ACL supports the following AKS capabilities: -- **Immutability**: The '/usr' directory is mounted as a read-only volume protected by dm-verity. At runtime, the kernel validates a signed root hash to detect and block tampering-- **Mandatory access control with SELinux**: ACL includes SELinux to enforce mandatory access control policies that restrict which processes can access sensitive system resources. Note that *SELinux is operating in enforcing mode by default. SELinux policies might evolve over time*.-- **Trusted Launch and Secure Boot**: ACL requires [Trusted Launch](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/trusted-launch) with Secure Boot and vTPM, to ensure the integrity of the boot chain before the OS loads. This is achieved using a Unified Kernel Image (UKI), which bundles the kernel, initramfs, and kernel command line into a single signed artifact.                                                                                                                                                                           @@ -2,45 +2,323 @@  ## Summary -This article discusses how to identify and resolve the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error (also known as error code ERR\_K8S\_API\_SERVER\_CONN\_FAIL, error number 51) that occurs when you try to start or create and deploy a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster.+This article describes how to identify and resolve the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error (also known as error code `ERR_K8S_API_SERVER_CONN_FAIL`, error number 51). This error might occur when you create, start, scale, or upgrade a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster or node pool.++When AKS provisions a Linux node, the node bootstrap script (delivered through the `vmssCSE` Custom Script Extension) checks whether the node can reach the cluster's Kubernetes API server on TCP port 443 before it starts the kubelet. If the node can resolve the API server address but can't establish a connection to it, the script exits with code 51, the node isn't registered in the cluster, and the operation fails.++In most cases, this error is caused by a network configuration in the customer's environment (such as a firewall, network security group, route table, proxy, or authorized IP range) that blocks or drops traffic from the node subnet to the API server.++Note++- This article applies to Linux nodes. If the node can't *resolve* the API server name, you receive a different error. For more information, see [Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFailVMExtensionError error code (52)](error-code-k8sapiserverdnslookupfailvmextensionerror). If the node can't reach required outbound endpoints such as `mcr.microsoft.com`, see [Troubleshoot the OutboundConnFailVMExtensionError error code (50)](error-code-outboundconnfailvmextensionerror).+- If your cluster uses [API Server VNet Integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration), a blocked connection to the API server usually causes a different error. See Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration.  ## Prerequisites -- The [Netcat](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/netcat) (nc) command-line tool+- [Azure CLI](/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli), signed in to the subscription that contains the AKS cluster.+- Permissions to read the AKS cluster and to run commands on the virtual machine scale sets (VMSS) or virtual machines (VMs) in the cluster's node resource group (for example, the [Virtual Machine Contributor](/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/built-in-roles/compute#virtual-machine-contributor) role).++The connectivity tests in this article run on the AKS nodes by using [Azure Run Command](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/run-command). They use the [curl](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html) command-line tool (or [Netcat](https://linuxcommandlibrary.com/man/netcat) (`nc`) for clusters that use API Server VNet Integration). These tools are already included in AKS Linux node images, so you don't have to install them on your local computer or on the nodes.  ## Symptoms -When you try to start or create an AKS cluster, you receive the following error message:-->-> Unable to establish connection from agents to Kubernetes API server, please see https://aka.ms/aks-required-ports-and-addresses for more information.->-> Details: Code="VMExtensionProvisioningError"->-> Message="VM has reported a failure when processing extension 'vmssCSE'.->-> Error message: "**Enable failed: failed to execute command: command terminated with exit status=51**\n[stdout]\n{->-> "ExitCode": "51",->-> "Output": "Thu Oct 14 18:07:37 UTC 2021,aks-nodepool1-18315663-vmss000000\nConnection to+When you try to create, start, scale, or upgrade an AKS cluster or node pool, the operation fails and you receive an error message that resembles the following example (identifiers are replaced with placeholders, and repeated progress output is removed):++```output+Code: K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError+Message: Create or update VMSS <vmss-resource-id> failed. Multiple VM extensions failed to be provisioned on the VM. The Extensions failed due to the errors:++[Extension Name: '<vmss-name>-AKSLinuxBilling'+Error Message: The handler for VM extension type 'Microsoft.AKS.Compute.AKS.Linux.Billing' has reported terminal failure for VM extension '<vmss-name>-AKSLinuxBilling' with error message: 'Dependent Extension Microsoft.Azure.Extensions.CustomScript did not succeed. Status was error'.]++[Extension Name: 'vmssCSE'+Error Message: VM has reported a user failure when processing extension 'vmssCSE'. Please correct the error and try again. (publisher 'Microsoft.Azure.Extensions' and type 'CustomScript'). Error code: '2'. Error message: 'failed to execute command: command terminated with exit status=51+[stdout]+{ "ExitCode": "51", "Output": "...+* connect to <api-server-ip> port 443 from <node-ip> port <port> failed: Connection timed out+* Failed to connect to <api-server-fqdn> port 443 after <n> ms: Couldn't connect to server+curl: (28) Failed to connect to <api-server-fqdn> port 443 after <n> ms: Couldn't connect to server+...+API server connection check code: 51++ exit 51", ... }+```++Key indicators of this error:++- The `vmssCSE` extension fails with `exit status=51` and the output contains `API server connection check code: 51`.+- The output shows a failed connection to the API server on port 443 (for example, `Connection timed out`, `Connection refused`, or `curl: (28) Failed to connect`).+- Other AKS extensions on the same VM (such as `AKSLinuxBilling`) might also fail with `Dependent Extension Microsoft.Azure.Extensions.CustomScript did not succeed`. This error is a side effect of the `vmssCSE` failure, not a separate problem.++In some API versions or tools, the message might begin with `Unable to establish connection from agents to Kubernetes API server, please see https://aka.ms/aks-required-ports-and-addresses for more information.` followed by `Code="VMExtensionProvisioningError"`.  ## Cause -Your cluster nodes can't connect to your cluster API server pod.+During node provisioning, the bootstrap script validates connectivity from the node to the API server before it starts the kubelet:++| Cluster configuration | Address that the node uses | Check performed by the bootstrap script |+| --- | --- | --- |+| Public cluster | Public API server FQDN (`<dns-prefix>-<hash>.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io`) | DNS lookup, then `curl https://<api-server-fqdn>:443` (with retries) |+| Private cluster | Private API server FQDN (for example, `<dns-prefix>-<hash>.<guid>.privatelink.<region>.azmk8s.io`) that resolves to the private endpoint IP | DNS lookup, then `curl https://<api-server-fqdn>:443` (with retries) |++If the DNS lookup fails, the script exits with code 52 or 53. If the DNS lookup succeeds but the TCP/TLS connection to port 443 can't be established within the retry period, the script exits with code 51.++The node must be able to reach the API server for AKS to work. This requirement is documented in [Outbound network and FQDN rules for AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/outbound-rules-control-egress#azure-global-required-fqdn--application-rules): `*.hcp.<location>.azmk8s.io` on HTTPS port 443 is required for node-to-API server communication.++Common reasons why the connection fails include:++- **Egress filtering blocks the API server.** A firewall, network virtual appliance (NVA), or proxy on the egress path doesn't allow TCP 443 to the API server FQDN (`*.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io`) or to the API server public IP address.+- **TLS inspection or a proxy interferes with the connection.** A device that intercepts, decrypts, or rewrites TLS traffic (including the Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) extension) to the API server breaks the connection.+- **Network security group (NSG) rules deny the traffic.** An outbound rule on the node subnet or NIC blocks TCP 443 from the nodes to the API server.+- **User-defined routes (UDRs) send traffic to the wrong next hop.** A route table on the node subnet sends API server traffic to an NVA that drops it, routes it asymmetrically, or has no path to the destination.+- **API server authorized IP ranges don't include the cluster's egress IP.** If [authorized IP ranges](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-authorized-ip-ranges) are enabled and the nodes egress through an IP address that isn't in the list (for example, the public IP of an Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, or other NVA), the API server rejects the connection.+- **(Private clusters) The private FQDN resolves to the wrong IP address.** Custom DNS servers or a manually managed private DNS zone return an outdated or incorrect IP address, so the node connects to an address where the API server isn't listening.+- **(Private clusters) The node can't reach the private endpoint.** For example, NSG rules or UDRs block traffic to the private endpoint IP, or the private endpoint is in a peered VNet that isn't reachable from the node subnet.  ## Solution -Run a Netcat command to verify that your nodes can resolve the cluster's fully qualified domain name (FQDN):+### Step 1: Gather cluster information++1. Get the API server endpoints and the network configuration of the cluster by running the [az aks show](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-show) command:++    ```azurecli+    az aks show \+        --resource-group <resource-group> \+        --name <cluster-name> \+        --query "{fqdn:fqdn, privateFqdn:privateFqdn, nodeResourceGroup:nodeResourceGroup, outboundType:networkProfile.outboundType, privateCluster:apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster, vnetIntegration:apiServerAccessProfile.enableVnetIntegration, authorizedIpRanges:apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIpRanges}" \+        --output json+    ```++    Use the output to determine the API server FQDN that the nodes use:++    - **Public cluster**: Use the `fqdn` value.+    - **Private cluster**: Use the `privateFqdn` value. If `privateFqdn` is empty (for example, when the private DNS zone is set to `none`), use the `fqdn` value.++    If `vnetIntegration` is `true`, see Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration instead.++    The error message usually contains the API server FQDN that the node tried to reach (for example, `Failed to connect to <api-server-fqdn> port 443`).+2. Identify the node pool instances that failed provisioning.++    - For node pools that use **Virtual Machine Scale Sets** (default):++        ```azurecli+        az vmss list \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --query "[].{name:name, nodePool:tags.\"aks-managed-poolName\", provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table++        az vmss list-instances \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --name <vmss-name> \+            --query "[].{instanceId:instanceId, name:name, provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table+        ```+    - For [Virtual Machines node pools](/en-us/azure/aks/virtual-machines-node-pools):++        ```azurecli+        az vm list \+            --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+            --query "[?tags.\"aks-managed-poolName\"=='<node-pool-name>'].{name:name, provisioningState:provisioningState}" \+            --output table+        ```++### Step 2: Test connectivity from the node to the API server++Because the node didn't register in the cluster, you can't use `kubectl debug` to access it. Instead, use [Azure Run Command](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/run-command) to run the same check that the bootstrap script runs.++Note++- The VM or VMSS instance must still exist and be running. If AKS already removed the failed instance, run the tests from a test VM that you deploy in the same node subnet (with the same NSG and route table).+- Run Command returns only the last 4,096 bytes of output, and only one Run Command can run on a VM at a time.+- The `--query "value[0].message" --output tsv` parameters in the following commands print the command output as readable text instead of JSON.++The following command is the same check that the bootstrap script runs. It sends an HTTPS request to the API server FQDN by using the cluster certificate authority (`/etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt`) that's already on the node. The verbose (`-v`) output shows the IP address that the FQDN resolves to and where the connection fails, so a separate DNS lookup isn't required. The `--max-time 30` parameter stops the test after 30 seconds if the API server doesn't respond.++- For a **Virtual Machine Scale Sets** node pool, run the [az vmss run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vmss/run-command#az-vmss-run-command-invoke) command:++    ```azurecli+    az vmss run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vmss-name> \+        --instance-id <instance-id> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "curl -v --max-time 30 --cacert /etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt https://<api-server-fqdn>:443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```+- For a **Virtual Machines** node pool, run the [az vm run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vm/run-command#az-vm-run-command-invoke) command:++    ```azurecli+    az vm run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vm-name> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "curl -v --max-time 30 --cacert /etc/kubernetes/certs/ca.crt https://<api-server-fqdn>:443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```++If the node can reach the API server, the `[stdout]` section contains an `Unauthorized` response from the API server, and the `[stderr]` section shows a successful connection. The `401` response is expected because the request is anonymous. The following example is abbreviated: -```shell-nc -vz <cluster-fqdn> 443+```output+Enable succeeded:+[stdout]+{+  "kind": "Status",+  "apiVersion": "v1",+  "metadata": {},+  "status": "Failure",+  "message": "Unauthorized",+  "reason": "Unauthorized",+  "code": 401+}+[stderr]+* Host <api-server-fqdn>:443 was resolved.+* IPv4: <api-server-ip>+*   Trying <api-server-ip>:443...+* Connected to <api-server-fqdn> (<api-server-ip>) port 443+...+*  SSL certificate verify ok.+...+< HTTP/2 401+... ``` -If you're using egress filtering through a firewall, make sure that traffic is allowed to your cluster FQDN.+If the node can't reach the API server, the `[stdout]` section is empty and curl reports the error at the end of the `[stderr]` section. For example:++```output+Enable succeeded:+[stdout]++[stderr]+* Host <api-server-fqdn>:443 was resolved.+* IPv4: <api-server-ip>+*   Trying <api-server-ip>:443...+* Connection timed out after 30001 milliseconds+* Closing connection+curl: (28) Connection timed out after 30001 milliseconds+```++Note++`Enable succeeded` only means that Run Command ran the script. It doesn't mean that the connectivity test passed.++#### Review the node provisioning log (optional)++To see the exact command and output of the failed check, review the end of the node provisioning log:++```azurecli+az vmss run-command invoke \+    --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+    --name <vmss-name> \+    --instance-id <instance-id> \+    --command-id RunShellScript \+    --scripts "grep -E 'curl -v --cacert|API server connection check code' /var/log/azure/cluster-provision.log | tail -n 20" \+    --query "value[0].message" \+    --output tsv+```++For a Virtual Machines node pool, use `az vm run-command invoke --resource-group <node-resource-group> --name <vm-name>` with the same `--command-id`, `--scripts`, `--query`, and `--output` values.++### Step 3: Interpret the results++| Result | Meaning | Next step |+| --- | --- | --- |+| curl returns an HTTP response (for example, `HTTP/2 401` with an `Unauthorized` status) | The node can now reach the API server. The issue might have been transient or already fixed. | Retry the operation (see Step 5). |+| `curl: (6) Could not resolve host` | The node can't resolve the API server name. | See [Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFailVMExtensionError error code (52)](error-code-k8sapiserverdnslookupfailvmextensionerror). |+| The IP address in the `IPv4:` or `Trying` line isn't the expected API server IP address (private clusters) | DNS returns an incorrect or outdated record. | Verify that the private DNS zone record matches the private endpoint IP and that custom DNS servers forward the zone to Azure DNS (`168.63.129.16`). See [Private AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/private-clusters). |+| `curl: (28)` (`Connection timed out` or `Operation timed out`) | Packets are dropped on the path (NSG, firewall, NVA, UDR, or authorized IP ranges). | Go to Step 4. |+| `curl: (7)` (`Connection refused`), `curl: (35)` or `curl: (56)` (`Connection reset by peer`) | A device on the path actively rejects or resets the connection, or the node connects to the wrong IP address. | Check firewalls, proxies, and NVAs on the path, and verify the resolved IP address. |+| A TLS error, such as `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem` or `curl: (35) ... unexpected eof while reading` | A proxy or TLS inspection device intercepts the connection. | Exclude the API server FQDN from TLS inspection, and don't modify the ALPN extension. |++### Step 4: Fix the network configuration++Based on the cluster configuration, verify the following items.++Tip++To check Azure networking resources (NSGs, route tables, Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, load balancer, and VNet peering) along the path from a node pool to a destination, you can also run a connectivity analysis by using [Azure Virtual Network Verifier](/en-us/azure/virtual-network-manager/concept-virtual-network-verifier). This tool doesn't evaluate third-party or on-premises devices.++#### Public clusters++- If you restrict egress traffic through a firewall or NVA, allow TCP 443 to `*.hcp.<region>.azmk8s.io` (application rule) or to the API server public IP address (network rule). For the complete list of requirements, see [Outbound network and FQDN rules for AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/outbound-rules-control-egress) and [Limit network traffic with Azure Firewall in AKS](/en-us/azure/aks/limit-egress-traffic).+- Make sure that NSGs on the node subnet and node NICs don't deny outbound TCP 443 to the API server.+- Make sure that TLS inspection and proxies don't intercept or alter traffic to the API server FQDN.+- If API server authorized IP ranges are enabled, make sure that the public IP address that the nodes use for egress (for example, the Azure Firewall, NAT gateway, or NVA public IP) is included. For more information, see [Secure access to the API server using authorized IP address ranges in AKS](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-authorized-ip-ranges).++#### Private clusters++- Verify that the API server FQDN resolves to the private endpoint IP address from the node subnet. If you use custom DNS servers, make sure that they forward the private DNS zone to Azure DNS (`168.63.129.16`) or otherwise return the correct record.+- Make sure that NSGs and UDRs on the node subnet allow traffic to the private endpoint IP address on TCP 443, and that the traffic isn't routed through an NVA that drops it.+- For more information, see [Create a private AKS cluster](/en-us/azure/aks/private-clusters).++### Step 5: Retry the operation++After you fix the network configuration, run the connectivity test from Step 2 again to confirm that the node can reach the API server. Then, retry the operation that failed (create, start, scale, or upgrade). If the cluster or node pool remains in a failed state, you can reconcile the cluster by running the [az aks update](/en-us/cli/azure/aks#az-aks-update) command without other parameters:++```azurecli+az aks update --resource-group <resource-group> --name <cluster-name>+```++## Clusters that use API Server VNet Integration++In clusters that use [API Server VNet Integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration), the nodes connect directly to the private IP address of the API server internal load balancer in the delegated API server subnet, without a DNS lookup. Get the private IP address of the API server. The IP address also appears in the error message (`nc -vz <api-server-ip> 443`).++    ```azurecli+    az network lb show \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name kube-apiserver \+        --query "frontendIPConfigurations[].privateIPAddress" \+        --output tsv+    ```+2. Test the connection from an affected node by running the same Netcat check that the bootstrap script runs. Use the [az vmss run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vmss/run-command#az-vmss-run-command-invoke) command for a Virtual Machine Scale Sets node pool, or the [az vm run-command invoke](/en-us/cli/azure/vm/run-command#az-vm-run-command-invoke) command for a Virtual Machines node pool:++    ```azurecli+    az vmss run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vmss-name> \+        --instance-id <instance-id> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "nc -vz -w 10 <api-server-ip> 443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```++    ```azurecli+    az vm run-command invoke \+        --resource-group <node-resource-group> \+        --name <vm-name> \+        --command-id RunShellScript \+        --scripts "nc -vz -w 10 <api-server-ip> 443" \+        --query "value[0].message" \+        --output tsv+    ```++    Netcat writes its result to the `[stderr]` section. A successful test shows `Connection to <api-server-ip> 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!`. A failed test shows an error such as `nc: connect to <api-server-ip> port 443 (tcp) timed out` or `nc: connect to <api-server-ip> port 443 (tcp) failed: Connection refused`.+3. If the test fails, check what blocks the traffic between the node subnet and the API server subnet:++    - Make sure that NSG rules on the node subnet, the node NICs, and the API server subnet allow the following communication:++        | Destination | Source | Protocol | Port |+        | --- | --- | --- | --- |+        | API server subnet CIDR | Cluster (node) subnet | TCP | 443 and 4443 |+        | API server subnet CIDR | Azure Load Balancer | TCP | 9988 |+    - Make sure that UDRs on the node subnet don't send traffic for the API server subnet through an NVA or firewall that drops it or routes it asymmetrically. -In rare cases, the firewall's outbound IP address can be blocked if you've authorized IP addresses that are enabled on your cluster. After you fix the network configuration, run the Netcat test again, and then retry the operation.  ## More information  - [General troubleshooting of AKS cluster creation issues](troubleshoot-aks-cluster-creation-issues)+- [Troubleshoot the OutboundConnFailVMExtensionError error code (50)](error-code-outboundconnfailvmextensionerror)+- [Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerDNSLookupFailVMExtensionError error code (52)](error-code-k8sapiserverdnslookupfailvmextensionerror)+- [Outbound network and FQDN rules for AKS clusters](/en-us/azure/aks/outbound-rules-control-egress)+- [API Server VNet Integration in AKS](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration)+- [Create a private AKS cluster](/en-us/azure/aks/private-clusters)+- [Run scripts in a Linux VM by using action Run Commands](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/linux/run-command)

                                                                                                                                                                                                            @@ -2,7 +2,7 @@  AI inference workloads don't behave like traditional stateless HTTP applications. Requests are often model-specific, long-running, expensive to serve, and sensitive to runtime signals such as accelerator availability, queue depth, request priority, token budget, and model server capacity. -Application Gateway for Containers inference gateway supports these workloads by integrating with the Kubernetes [Gateway API Inference Extension](https://gateway-api-inference-extension.sigs.k8s.io/), which adds inference-aware resources to the Gateway API model. By using the inference gateway, you can expose self-hosted model servers through Application Gateway for Containers with model-aware and load-aware routing behavior.+Application Gateway for Containers inference gateway supports these workloads by integrating with the Kubernetes [Gateway API Inference Extension](https://gateway-api-inference-extension.sigs.k8s.io/), which adds inference-aware backends to the Gateway API model. By using the inference gateway, you can expose self-hosted model servers through Application Gateway for Containers with model-aware and load-aware routing behavior.  The inference gateway is purpose-built for serving large language models (LLMs) and other inference workloads. It routes requests based on model server signals rather than generic load balancing, which lowers time to first token (TTFT), reduces timeouts under load, and improves GPU efficiency. Built on the ingress capabilities of Application Gateway for Containers, the inference gateway also lets you pair AI workloads with capabilities like the web application firewall (WAF) to secure traffic before it reaches your model servers. @@ -12,24 +12,50 @@ Important  The Application Gateway for Containers inference gateway is currently in preview. See the [Supplemental Terms of Use for Microsoft Azure Previews](https://azure.microsoft.com/support/legal/preview-supplemental-terms/) for legal terms that apply to Azure features that are in beta, preview, or otherwise not yet released into general availability. -## What the Gateway API Inference Extension provides+## Building blocks of the inference gateway -The Gateway API Inference Extension turns a Gateway API implementation into an inference gateway by adding inference-specific backend and scheduling concepts.+An inference gateway combines three parts: a Gateway API implementation that handles ingress, an `InferencePool` backend defined by the Gateway API Inference Extension, and an endpoint picker that chooses a model server pod for each request. Application Gateway for Containers provides the first part and a managed body-based routing processor. You provide the `InferencePool` and the endpoint picker in your cluster. -The extension introduces these primary resources and components:+- **InferencePool**: A backend resource (`inference.networking.k8s.io/v1`) that represents a group of model server pods, the port they serve on, and a reference to the endpoint picker that selects a pod for each inference request.+- **Endpoint Picker (EPP)**: The role, defined by the Gateway API Inference Extension, of the component that selects an endpoint for each request. The gateway calls the EPP by using the endpoint picker protocol defined by the extension. The EPP returns the model server pod that should serve the request. This resource filters Hubble metrics; it isn't a filter for every node-level metric exported by the cluster.++For your first configuration, follow the application example below from start to finish. After that, choose another task:++| Task | Configuration |+| --- | --- |+| **Filter DNS requests and replies for a client** | Use `dns` with source and destination filters. See Select DNS requests and replies. |+| **Filter TCP metrics by workload** | Use `tcp` with pod or label selectors. See Select workloads by label. |+| **Filter HTTP metrics for an application** | Use `httpV2` with workload filters. See Select HTTP observations for an application. |+| **Filter an existing metric by identity** | See Filter flow metrics by security identity. |+| **Exclude a workload from drop metrics** | Use `drop` with an exclude filter. See Exclude a workload from drop metrics. |+| **See external destination IP addresses in metrics** | See Inspect TCP traffic to external destinations. |+| **See destination ports in metrics** | See Inspect destination ports. |++Filters choose which traffic contributes to each metric. If you omit a service-provided metric from the resource, it remains enabled without a CNM filter for that metric. For example, `checkout-` matches `checkout-7f6d8b9c5-x2abc`, but not `payments-7f6d8b9c5-x2abc`.++```bash+NAMESPACE="production"+POD_PREFIX="checkout-"+CLIENT_POD="<running-pod-with-curl>"+TEST_URL="https://<approved-host>/"+kubectl get pod -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" -o wide+kubectl exec -n "$NAMESPACE" "$CLIENT_POD" -- curl --version ``` -### Get cluster credentials+Confirm that the pod is running and `curl` is available. Only one CRD can exist per cluster, and changes take approximately 30 seconds to reconcile. To configure another metric, add an entry under `spec.filters`. If that metric already has an entry, update that entry instead of adding a duplicate.++For example, if you already filter `dns` and want to enable `flows-to-world`, keep the `dns` entry and add a `flows-to-world` entry beside it. Don't replace the DNS configuration with the new example.++### Filter flow metrics for one application++This example counts flow observations that come from the selected application's pods. Other source pods don't match this filter. It changes only the `flow` metric. It doesn't enable the optional metrics or change traffic permissions.++#### If the resource doesn't exist++Run this Bash command to create `network-metrics.yaml`. Bash replaces `${NAMESPACE}` and `${POD_PREFIX}` with the values you set above:++```bash+cat > network-metrics.yaml <<EOF apiVersion: acn.azure.com/v1alpha1 kind: ContainerNetworkMetric metadata:-  name: : container-network-metric # Cluster scoped+  name: container-network-metric spec:   filters:-  - metric: flow-    includeFilters: # List of include filters-      - name: sample-filter # Filter name-        from:-          namespacedPod: # List of source namespace/pods.
